P1.evidence: The only genuine setter read-back in the batch, and it was used twice: 'I was talking to Kim. I think you spoke with him a couple of days ago... he briefed me in a little bit about your situation... Kim mentioned that you've been working out, doing all sorts of stuff throughout the whole life, correct?' and later 'Kim also mentioned that your nutrition is also on spot, like, you're doing carb cycling. Is that correct?' The prospect visibly felt seen. The frame was a two-part fit frame rather than the scripted four — 'I would love to hear it also from you, like to get in more depth, in detail. And then we can assess whether we are a fit for you, or not, that's totally fine too' — and no agreement was requested on it.

P2.evidence: Training history was worked thoroughly — 'what specifically, and what are you doing currently in terms of fitness' opened a full inventory of yoga, calisthenics, movement school, handstands and the 12-week strength block, and 'did you like the results? Like, did you get the result that you wanted?' closed it properly. Work was asked ('Does business take a lot of a big chunk of time from your week?'). But age, height and weight were never asked — the 175 lb figure had to be inferred from an aside about calisthenics being harder at his current bodyweight — and health conditions were never raised at all. Limitations got one narrow question, 'do you feel any stiffnesses in your body in any particular areas?', which surfaced the ankles but not injuries or duration. Nutrition was confirmed off the setter's notes rather than opened up. Sleep only appeared because the prospect volunteered that dance weekends wreck it, and energy was never touched.

P3.evidence: The strongest goals work in the batch. The surface goal was named and legitimised rather than dismissed ('I know it's, like you said, it's kind of a vain goal, but getting lean'), then the bridge question was asked cleanly and openly: 'when you got leaner? Is there anything that's opening up for you? Something that wasn't possible? Or is it just proving yourself that you can do it?' That produced the real answer — 'I think it's just the discipline and proving myself that you can do it' — which is identity, not aesthetics. The can't-do-it-now goal came out in the same exchange (handstand push-ups and shoulder presses given up at 175 lb). The reflect-back is the best single move in these twelve files: 'the effort alone stopped producing the next level that you're trying to get. The game now, from what I'm hearing, is precision and dialing in those small pieces and just tweaking that. You operate as an athlete right now.' The prospect accepted and expanded it. Marked down only because 'who else does that impact' and the moving-better consequence were both delivered as assertions about other clients rather than asked, though the prospect answered them anyway ('I'm more focused, more present for people').

P4.evidence: Past attempts were genuinely inventoried and probed — 'you've basically been around... You've tried it all, except kettlebells, which is interesting, because did you do CrossFit, for example?' followed by the results question. The root cause was then diagnosed FOR the prospect rather than drawn out of him: 'for me, it definitely doesn't sound like an effort issue at all, right? Because you're doing a lot' and 'the game now is precision'. The diagnosis was correct and the prospect endorsed it, and he separately named his own gap unprompted — 'I'm so used to being able to get a program and then organize it myself. Being able to receive somebody else's help and support, I know how important that is.' But the script credits asking, and the rep asserted. The one place the why was pushed on, the failure to get lean, got a shrug ('it was never my body type... bulking was easy. Cutting was like dialing it in') and was not pursued.

P5.evidence: Not run in any form. No two-year question, no willingness-to-settle, no why-not, no line in the sand. Worth noting that this is the exact prospect type Chris Klevan taught the team to handle three hours after this call ended — 'it's not really a cost of inaction. It's a cost of staying good... dude, most people want to get to the level that you're at. And so for you, if you were to stay exactly as you are, why is that not enough for you?' That reframe was available and, on this call, unknown to the rep. The material for it was sitting there: he loves where his body is at and has never got lean in twenty years of trying.

P6.evidence: The belief question was asked close to script and got a substantial answer: 'if you had the right training and simple nutrition, and the real accountability from Trevor built around your life, do you believe that you would get finally to your goals and get leaner and ingrain this skill set?' The prospect answered at length and volunteered the deeper reason he wants coaching. The go-all-in isolation was never asked, which matters here because it is the same question that would have isolated finances before the payment conversation started — instead the money discussion opened cold when the prospect asked about instalments.

P11.evidence: Step 1 only partly done: $2,000 of $6,000 collected and confirmed ('it just said invoice paid, $2,000'), with the remaining $4,000 resting on a verbal 'yeah, let's do that' — no dates, no autopay, no schedule. Step 2 clean: Trevor booked for 11:45am the next day with the invite confirmed. Step 3 failed outright — the agreement did not exist and the rep found out live: 'this is totally custom-built. You don't have the agreement right now. I'll need to craft it myself, and I will send it later on today.' The client paid with nothing signed. Step 4 was described correctly ('get the agreement done, fill out the onboarding form also') and the Skool invitation was referenced, but the email it was supposed to arrive in turned out not to contain what the rep said it contained, so the prospect ended the call unsure what he had.

objection_plays.detail: The most complete money play in the batch, though the trigger was a logistics question rather than resistance — 'Is that one-time payment? Is that able to be broken up into other forms of payments?' Ran: the scripted upfront-versus-plan framing ('Most of the guys just put it on a credit card up front, but like, do you feel like you need a payment plan?'); permission to talk openly ('let's just openly talk about what's possible to put down today, and how we can structure that in the future'); monthly surplus ('when you pay all the bills, groceries, mortgage, whatever you have, roughly how much do you have left in the tank?'); savings and investments ('in terms of savings... I know you cannot move the 401k'); credit cards and available limit ('And how about credit cards?'). Did not run: the isolation question, which the playbook puts first and in capitals — finances were never set aside to check nothing else was blocking. Also missing: the SHOULD I versus HOW reframe, the number of cards, and used-versus-available. The rep then structured to capacity across four attempts — $1,200/month with interest, Payva financing (declined), a manager-relayed 50/50 split, and finally three interest-free $2,000 instalments.

A real fear-and-doubt trigger landed early and was not played: 'a part of me has little doubts like but can I get that same stimulus of anabolic stimulus from just kettlebells from like the squats.' The rep said 'Yeah, but it's different' and moved straight into his own hip-dysplasia story. None of the scripted moves ran — no certainty question, no bridge, no plane. The prospect self-resolved with 'I'll just trust, you know, you don't know, you got to find out', so it never became an obstacle, but the substantive question of whether kettlebells build muscle the way loaded squats do went unanswered for a man whose stated goal is body composition.

notes: Discovery and goals were run at a level the rest of this batch does not reach — the setter read-back, the past-attempts work and the 'precision, not effort' reflect-back are all worth clipping for training. Two things to fix. First, the consequence frame is missing again, and here the optimizer version ('why is staying good not enough for you?') was exactly the tool needed. Second, the close: three different prices were live, the cheapest was landed on by accident, no isolation preceded the money conversation, and the client paid $2,000 against a $6,000 commitment with no agreement in existence and no schedule for the balance.
